---
title: "Quiz: matching objects"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. IoU = overlap / union of two objects; matching is one to one at an IoU threshold $\tau$; TP = matched pairs, FP = unmatched predictions, FN = unmatched true objects.

---

**Q1.** Why is there no "true negative" when we count objects, and what does that mean for accuracy and ROC curves?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What would a true-negative object be?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A true negative would be "background correctly not predicted as an object", but the background is not made of countable objects. So object-level scores use only TP, FP and FN: precision, recall, F1, matching accuracy. Accuracy $(TP + TN)/\text{all}$ and the false-positive rate $FP/(FP + TN)$ of a ROC curve are undefined; precision–recall curves take their place.
:::

---

**Q2.** A nucleus of radius 3 px is predicted one pixel off; a nucleus of radius 20 px too. Which prediction is more likely to fail at $\tau = 0.5$, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the lost overlap with the area of the object.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The small one. A one-pixel shift loses a strip of about one pixel times the diameter: a large fraction of a small object (IoU about 0.65 for radius 3 px) and a small fraction of a large one (about 0.94 for 20 px). With a little extra outline error the small object falls below 0.5. Small objects need a lower $\tau$ or a different criterion (e.g. distance between centres).
:::

---

**Q3.** At $\tau = 0.6$, can one true object have two predictions with IoU $\ge \tau$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How much of the true object must each of them cover?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. IoU above 0.5 means the prediction overlaps more than half of the true object. Two non-overlapping predictions cannot both cover more than half of it. So above 0.5 every object has at most one candidate, and the matching is forced: no greedy-versus-optimal question.
:::

---

**Q4.** A true nucleus is split by the method into two halves, each with IoU 0.4 with it. What are its contributions to TP, FP and FN at $\tau = 0.5$? And at $\tau = 0.3$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One to one: at most one half can be matched.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At $\tau = 0.5$: no half matches, so 0 TP, 2 FP, 1 FN. At $\tau = 0.3$: one half matches (TP), the other is an FP: 1 TP, 1 FP, 0 FN.
:::

---

**Q5.** Method A has F1 0.92 at $\tau = 0.5$ and 0.30 at $\tau = 0.8$; method B has 0.80 and 0.75. Which would you use to count cells, and which to measure their areas?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a high $\tau$ demand?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A finds more objects (better at 0.5) but with sloppy outlines (collapses at 0.8): better for **counting**. B's outlines are tight (holds up at 0.8), but it misses or merges more objects: better for **measuring** areas and shapes of the objects it finds. One F1 at one $\tau$ would have hidden this.
:::

---

**Q6.** A method predicts 20 objects with scores; 4 low-scored specks at the end of the list are false positives. Why does removing them change F1 but hardly change AP?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where in the sorted list are they, and what happens to recall there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
F1 counts all predictions at the chosen cut-off: 4 fewer FP raise precision and F1. AP is the area under the precision–recall curve built by walking down the list by score; the specks come after all true objects are found, so they do not increase recall and add (almost) no area. AP rewards a good **ranking**; a method can have a high AP and still need a good score cut-off.
:::

---

**Q7.** Paper X reports "AP$_{0.5}$ = 0.80" for nucleus segmentation, paper Y "AP$_{0.5}$ = 0.88" for detection. Can you conclude that Y is better?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The same name is used for two quantities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Cell-segmentation papers often write AP for $TP/(TP + FP + FN)$ at one $\tau$ (the matching accuracy in this course); detection papers mean the area under a precision–recall curve of scored predictions. The two numbers are on different scales even for the same result (in the lecture's example: 0.5 versus 0.69). Besides, they are measured on different data.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the object F1 equals $2\,TP/(n_G + n_P)$, where $n_G$ and $n_P$ are the numbers of true and predicted objects. Why does this make F1$(\tau)$ non-increasing?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Every predicted object is either TP or FP.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$n_P = TP + FP$ and $n_G = TP + FN$, so $2\,TP + FP + FN = n_G + n_P$, which does not depend on $\tau$. Raising $\tau$ removes allowed pairs, so the number of matches can only stay or drop; F1 is that number divided by a constant.
:::
